reasoning: The country name always carries the article: il-yuunaan, with long uu then aa. ي is a consonant glide here, so the article stays il-.
Ends in a long aa in pause, the taa marbuta surfacing only in construct, as in zakaat il-fiTr. The standard religious term in Ramallah.
Emphatic ط doubled whole by the shadda: baTTal. Used both for quitting something and, before another verb, for 'no longer', as in baTTal yiiji.
Sukun on ه then taa marbuta as e after ج: lahje. It covers 'dialect' as much as 'accent'.
Short i then a final cluster: nimr, plural nmuura. Also a common man's name.
A fixed condolence formula, so it keeps its Form II shadda on ظ, written TH; Ramallah speakers realise that sound as an emphatic z. Said to the bereaved family, plural addressee.
Form X passive participle with Palestinian i in the prefix: mista3mal, not MSA musta3mal. Standard for secondhand goods.
shu is the Palestinian 'what' and the b-imperfect bti- marks the ordinary present, addressed to a man. The question mark is not romanized.
ح is 7, and the Palestinian masculine form is 7ilu with i then u. Sweet in taste, and also 'nice / pretty' of people and things.
b-imperfect of kaffa with shadda on ف and the object suffix -ni: bikaffiini, literally 'it suffices me'.
ع plus the article contracts to 3al-, and il-balad is what Ramallah people call the town centre. law sama7t is the everyday 'please' to a man.
ح is 7 and the taa marbuta after م is e: ma7kame. Ordinary word for a law court, MSA in origin but fully colloquial.
First short vowel drops, leaving an initial cluster: zbaale, taa marbuta as e after ل. The usual Ramallah word for rubbish.
Past verb plus -ni, then the Palestinian complementiser inno with shadda on ن and final o. Word-initial hamza is written as the vowel i.
khalliini 'let me' with shadda on ل; the following verb is bare subjunctive afakkir. barja3lak is the b-imperfect with -lak, 'I'll come back to you (m.)'.

vowelled_arabic: اللِّي عَلَى رَاسُو بَطْحَة بِحَسِّس عَلَيْهَا
reasoning: illi is the Palestinian relative, raaso 'his head' with the -o suffix. baT7a is a bump or dent, and bi7assis is the Form II b-imperfect 'he keeps feeling it'; in speech 3ala often reduces to 3a.
Long ii: miin, the Palestinian 'who', against MSA man.
ث is t, so ثاني is respelled تَانِي. ع plus the article assimilates to the sun letter ش: 3ash-shimaal.
Read as the imperative khalli, which is what the English gloss implies; as past tense it would be khalla. timshi here is 'go along, take their course'.
First person past of zihi', with the first vowel dropped and ق as a glottal stop: zhi't. Said with feeling it carries the 'I'm so fed up' sense.
Short i then long aa: libnaan, without the article.
3een has ee, with the possessive -o: 3eeno. The feminine adjective loses its short vowel, waas3a, taa marbuta as a after ع. Idiomatic for greedy or covetous.
rii7a plus -o gives rii7to, 'its smell'. zaakye is the Palestinian word for a lovely smell or taste, taa marbuta as e after ي.
ma negates the verb, ri7t is first person past of raa7. The hamza inside la'inno is written since it follows a prefix; 3ashaan is an equally common Ramallah 'because'.
Plain Form I past fata7 with 3een, ee not ii, plus -o. Idiomatically 'he wised up / became alert'; as an imperative ifta7 3eenak means 'watch out'.
